name: Hadrosaurus foulkii
tenure: Mounted in 1868, the first mounted dinosaur skeleton anywhere. The current cast mount was built for a 2008 exhibit, stored in 2020, and returned to the floor on July 16, 2025.
facts: Bones were first noticed in 1838 by John Estaugh Hopkins in a marl pit in Haddonfield, New Jersey.
William Parker Foulke excavated the skeleton in 1858 and Joseph Leidy of the Academy described it.
Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins built the 1868 mount, the first to show a dinosaur standing on two legs.
Crowds grew so large after the mount went up that the Academy began charging admission.
Hadrosaurus foulkii has been the New Jersey state dinosaur since 1991.
The original fossil bones are kept in the Academy's vertebrate paleontology collection.
Collections manager Ned Gilmore, 2025: "Hadrosaurus foulkii, or Haddy, is a bit of a local celebrity."

image.credit: James Capaldi, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
image.alt: The mounted Hadrosaurus foulkii cast standing on two legs in Dinosaur Hall

name: Dinosaur Hall
tenure: The Academy's first dinosaur hall, Discovering Dinosaurs, opened in 1986. The current Dinosaur Hall opened in 1998 and was refreshed in 2018.
facts: The hall held more than 30 species of dinosaurs and other Mesozoic reptiles, about half of them as full skeletal mounts.
Mounts included Tyrannosaurus rex, Hadrosaurus, Avaceratops, Chasmosaurus, Corythosaurus, Pachycephalosaurus and the mosasaur Tylosaurus.
Visitors could touch a real Tyrannosaurus rex bone and a dinosaur footprint.
The hall included a Torosaurus skull, an Ichthyosaurus slab and dinosaur eggs.

image.credit: Jon Voltaire B. Aquino, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
image.alt: The Tyrannosaurus rex cast at the entrance to Dinosaur Hall

name: Tyrannosaurus rex
tenure: On the floor since the Discovering Dinosaurs exhibit opened in 1986.
facts: The Academy described its Tyrannosaurus rex as up to 42 feet long and weighing an estimated 7.5 tons.
The skeleton is a cast of specimen AMNH 5027 from the American Museum of Natural History in New York.
It stood at the entrance to Dinosaur Hall as the first thing visitors saw.

image.credit: Jon Voltaire B. Aquino, Wikimedia Commons, public domain
image.alt: The Tyrannosaurus rex cast in Dinosaur Hall

name: The Big Dig
facts: A hands-on fossil dig inside Dinosaur Hall where visitors brushed away sediment to uncover fossils.
The dig was modeled on the badlands of New Mexico.

name: Outside In
facts: A discovery center for children ages 3 to 8 with live animals including a leopard tortoise, a leopard gecko and a box turtle.
Children could climb into a giant nest and dig for shark teeth.
It housed the Cheryl Beth Silverman Hands-on Lab.

name: The dioramas
tenure: Most of the 37 dioramas were built between the 1930s and the 1960s. Two were renovated in 2018.
facts: The first floor held North American animals including bison, musk ox, bears and moose.
The second floor held African and Asian animals including a lion, zebras, an okapi, a gorilla, tigers, a takin, a kiang, pandas and a yak.
The third floor held extinct species including the passenger pigeon and the Labrador duck.

image.alt: A Serengeti diorama at the Academy of Natural Sciences

name: Secrets of the Dioramas
facts: An exhibit on how the dioramas were made, covering taxidermy, plant models and painted backgrounds.
It stood on the second floor across from the kiang diorama.

name: Native Plants on the Parkway
facts: An outdoor native plant garden on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, titled A Botany of Nations Garden.
It was created with the Garden Club of Philadelphia and Forrester Landscape Studio.

name: Botany of Nations
facts: An exhibit built around seven plant specimens from the Lewis and Clark Herbarium and the Indigenous knowledge connected to them.

name: Neighborhood Naturalists
facts: An exhibit about community science and the City Nature Challenge.

name: What Eats What
facts: A display of a stream food chain featuring a brook trout and a mayfly.

name: Science at the Academy
facts: A display on the Academy's research that included a Tiktaalik roseae fossil, the fish with limb-like fins described by Academy scientists.

name: Marveling at Mollusks
facts: A display of about 100 mollusk specimens drawn from the Academy's malacology collection.

name: Butterflies!
tenure: Opened in October 2006. It closed during the pandemic and never reopened.
facts: A tropical garden where live butterflies flew freely around visitors.
It closed with the pandemic in 2020 and did not reopen.

name: Live Animal Center
facts: A center housing about 100 animals, most of them rescued, visible through glass near the 19th Street entrance.

name: Fossil Prep Lab
facts: A working laboratory where visitors watched technicians prepare fossils, including material from the Morrison Formation in Montana.

name: The Deinonychus bronze
hall: Outside at 19th Street and the Parkway
facts: A bronze Deinonychus by sculptor Kent Ullberg stands outside the building at 19th Street and the Benjamin Franklin Parkway.
It was installed in 1987.

image.alt: The bronze Deinonychus outside the Academy of Natural Sciences

name: Deinonychus and Tenontosaurus
facts: A mount in Dinosaur Hall showed a pack of Deinonychus attacking a Tenontosaurus.

image.alt: The Deinonychus mount in Dinosaur Hall

name: Corythosaurus
facts: Unlike most of the hall's casts, the Corythosaurus mount is mostly original bone with a lightweight cast skull.
It was the centerpiece of the Academy's fossil hall for much of the twentieth century.

name: Tylosaurus
facts: A mount of the giant marine reptile Tylosaurus, a mosasaur that could reach about 43 feet.
It hung in Dinosaur Hall alongside the predatory fish Xiphactinus.

image.credit: Jonathan Chen, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
image.alt: The Tylosaurus mount in Dinosaur Hall

name: Megalonyx jeffersonii claws
facts: Fossil claws of Jefferson's ground sloth, Megalonyx jeffersonii, a species first described from bones studied by Thomas Jefferson and Caspar Wistar.

name: The Lewis and Clark Herbarium
tenure: Deposited at the Academy in the 1890s.
facts: The herbarium holds 226 pressed plant sheets collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, representing 173 species, 55 of them type specimens.
It is a research collection rather than a permanent public display.

name: The 1852 mummies
facts: In 1852 the Academy displayed four human mummies along with George Gliddon's mummified calf, two hawks, six ibis and 32 serpents.

name: The research collections
tenure: Built up since the Academy's founding in 1812.
facts: The Academy holds about 19 million specimens and more than 73,000 type specimens.
Major collections include 1.6 million fish specimens, 10 million mollusks and more than 215,000 birds, plus a diatom herbarium, entomology, and vertebrate and invertebrate fossils.
The Academy said in September 2026 that access to and use of the collections will not be affected by the museum's closure.

name: The Library and Archives
facts: The library holds more than 75,000 titles, with material dating from the 16th century onward.
